## Not every outside note is going somewhere

Lessons 52 and 53 taught you to read a chromatic pitch as a signpost. Here are
two grammars where it isn't one. *Modal mixture* borrows from the parallel major
or minor while keeping the same tonic. In C major, F minor comes straight out of
C minor, and its A-flat slides down to G on the way back to C. No new tonic. You
borrowed a colour.

The blues runs on a rule of its own: dominant sevenths on I, IV and V alike.
Everywhere else a dominant seventh points a fifth downward; here it's stable
colour, even on I. So when an outside note turns up, ask what it does next. Does
it press toward a target, borrow a lowered degree, or follow another style's
rules? The pitch alone can't tell you.

## Minor iv, then twelve bars of sevenths

Major IV sits next to borrowed minor iv on the way back to I. Then a twelve-bar
blues, stored as degrees, each rendered as a dominant seventh in C.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 82
use_synth :piano

[:c3, :f3, :f3, :c3].zip([:major, :major, :minor, :major]).each do |root, quality|
  play_chord chord(root, quality), release: 1.8, amp: 0.75
  sleep 2
end

sleep 2

twelve_bar = [1, 1, 1, 1, 4, 4, 1, 1, 5, 4, 1, 5]
degree_offsets = {1 => 0, 4 => 5, 5 => 7}
tonic = note(:c3)

twelve_bar.each do |degree|
  root = tonic + degree_offsets[degree]
  play_chord chord(root, :dom7), release: 1.8, amp: 0.72
  sleep 2
end
```

When F major turns into F minor, A drops to A-flat, and your step back to G
contracts to a semitone. That contraction is the borrowed chord's route home. In
the blues, every root carries a major third and a minor seventh, C7 included, so
the friction never resolves.

## Strip the quality, move the tonic

1. Replace F minor with A-flat major before the final C. Both come from C minor,
   both contain A-flat, and the bass routes into C differ. Which one gets you
   home with more weight?
2. Change `:dom7` to `:major` in the blues renderer. The degrees are untouched,
   so the sevenths are the only casualty. How much of the blues was in the form,
   and how much in the quality?
3. Set `tonic` to `note(:e3)`, then `note(:a2)`. Degrees and offsets hold still.
   The form transposes faithfully; register changes the weight of identical
   voicings.

## Lowered degrees colour, raised degrees point

Parallel keys share a tonic and disagree about the scale between. Borrow from
parallel minor and you pull flat 3, flat 6 and flat 7 into major. Minor iv
carries flat 6, whose semitone descent to degree 5 is the voice leading you just
heard.

So here's your first question about any chromatic note: raised or lowered?
Secondary dominants raise one and aim it somewhere. Borrowed chords lower one
and colour the motion around a tonic that hasn't budged. It's a heuristic, and
it fails often enough to keep you honest.

Your form lives in the degree array because form transposes. Giving every root
the same seventh quality makes I7 visible as a rule of the style, not an
exception patched into a quality table. Treat the array as one model. Sources
vary in length, turnaround and substitutions; when a recording disagrees, encode
what it does.

## Two chromatic phrases, side by side

Render one twelve-bar degree array in C, E and A without copying its form data.
Then write a four-bar phrase in a major key with one borrowed chord, commenting
every chromatic pitch with its source. Put it beside a secondary-dominant phrase
from [Lesson 52](52-secondary-dominants.qmd) and listen for the difference: a note that pulls somewhere, a
note that changes the light.
